items.headline: US jury convicts Huawei on 10 of 12 counts in trade secrets and sanctions case
items.what: A jury in a Brooklyn federal court convicted Huawei and three subsidiaries on 10 of 12 criminal counts, including bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations and conspiracy to steal trade secrets from US companies. The jury acquitted the company on the two most serious counts, racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice. Sentencing is set for September 14, 2027. Prosecutors said Huawei stole router source code from Cisco, antenna technology from Quintel and other technology from US companies, and deceived banks about its business in Iran.
items.why: The verdict ends a case that began in 2018 and sits at the center of the US China technology dispute.

items.headline: US Treasury financial crimes unit reports unauthorized access to its systems
items.what: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, the US Treasury bureau that collects suspicious activity reports from banks, said it is investigating a cybersecurity incident after an unauthorized party gained access to a limited subset of its systems. FinCEN took some systems offline as a precaution. Banks can still file suspicious activity reports online, and the bureau hotline for time sensitive reports is unaffected. FinCEN has not said which systems were reached, whether any data was taken, when the intrusion began or who was behind it. It also issued an order giving some filers until December 30 to submit reports that were due between November 18 and December 29.
items.why: FinCEN holds sensitive financial transaction data used by law enforcement to track money laundering and terrorist financing, so unauthorized access to its systems raises questions about the protection of that data. The disclosure came the same day as reports of a separate breach at US intelligence agencies, adding to scrutiny of government network security.

items.headline: European Commission proposes a Quantum Act and a 50 billion euro tech fund
items.what: The European Commission proposed a Quantum Act on Wednesday, a draft law meant to turn European quantum research into products and services, strengthen supply chains and prepare digital systems for post-quantum cryptography. The proposal also lays the groundwork for a Sovereign Tech Equity Fund, which the Commission says would provide equity financing for technologies central to European tech independence. EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said officials are targeting 50 billion euros for the fund. The draft law still needs agreement from EU member states and the European Parliament before it can become law.
items.why: Europe trails the United States and China in AI, chips and cloud computing, and the proposal is the bloc's main move to close that gap in quantum technology. The fund would be one of the largest public tech investment vehicles in Europe, and the procurement rules would favour European companies.
